A tripeptide made from three **different** amino acids is a chain of three residues, and the
question is how many distinct **orders** they can be joined in.
A peptide chain has **direction** — one end has a free amino group (the N-terminal) and the
other a free carboxyl (the C-terminal) — so A–B–C and C–B–A are **different** peptides. The
count is therefore the number of **permutations** of three things:
**3! = 3 × 2 × 1 = 6** ✓
Writing them out with amino acids A, B and C:
A–B–C, A–C–B, B–A–C, B–C–A, C–A–B, C–B–A
six in all, each a distinct compound with its own properties.
The answer would be **3** — option (a) — only if the chain had no direction, so that each
sequence and its reverse were the same thing. They are not, and that directionality is why
the primary structure of a protein must always be written and read **N-terminal to
C-terminal**.

24, five give 120, and a modest protein of 100 residues drawn from 20 amino acids has 20¹⁰⁰
possible sequences. That is the scale of variety the genetic code has to specify, and the
reason proteins can do so many different things.

Denaturation breaks the **weak** forces that hold a protein in shape but leaves the
**covalent** backbone intact. So the structure that survives is the one made of covalent
bonds — the **primary** structure ✓.
Taking the four levels in turn:
**Primary** — the **sequence of amino acids**, joined by **peptide (covalent) bonds**. Heat and
pH changes cannot break these, so the sequence is **unaffected** ✓
**Secondary** — the α-helix and β-sheet, held by **hydrogen bonds**. These break easily;
the helix unwinds ✗
**Tertiary** — the overall three-dimensional fold, held by hydrogen bonds, hydrophobic
interactions, salt bridges and **disulphide** bonds. Destroyed ✗
**Quaternary** — the assembly of several chains into one functional unit, held by the same
weak forces. The subunits separate ✗
So denaturation reduces a protein to a random coil with its sequence intact — which is why
the biological activity is lost even though no amino acid has been removed.
The familiar examples are the coagulation of egg white on boiling and the curdling of milk
with acid. Neither can be undone, because although the sequence survives, the chain cannot
find its way back to the one correct fold out of the enormous number available.

destroy the primary structure.

The hormone that governs the **rate at which the body burns fats, proteins and carbohydrates**
— the **basal metabolic rate** — is **thyroxine** ✓, secreted by the **thyroid** gland.
Thyroxine (T₄) and its more active form triiodothyronine (T₃) act on almost every tissue,
speeding up the oxidation of foodstuffs and so the release of energy and heat. Their effects
show directly in metabolic disease:
**hyperthyroidism** — too much: weight loss despite a good appetite, rapid heartbeat,
intolerance of heat
**hypothyroidism** — too little: weight gain, lethargy, feeling cold, and **goitre** where
the cause is iodine deficiency
Thyroxine is also the **iodine-containing** hormone, with four iodine atoms in the molecule,
which is why dietary iodine matters and why salt is iodised.
The other options have narrower jobs:
**(c) Insulin** regulates **blood glucose** specifically, promoting its uptake and storage as
glycogen. It controls where sugar goes, not the overall rate of energy release.
**(b) Adrenaline** is the short-term 'fight or flight' hormone, raising heart rate and blood
glucose for minutes, not the sustained metabolic rate.
**(d) Cortisone** is a steroid, anti-inflammatory, involved in the stress response.
∴ thyroxine.

Note: the printed key gives (c), insulin. Insulin controls blood sugar; the hormone that sets
the rate of burning fats, proteins and carbohydrates is thyroxine, so the key is wrong and
has been corrected to (a).

The hormone that converts glucose into glycogen is **insulin** ✓, secreted by the **β-cells**
of the islets of Langerhans in the pancreas.
When blood glucose rises after a meal, insulin is released and does three things: it promotes
the **uptake** of glucose into muscle and fat cells, it stimulates the liver and muscles to
store it as **glycogen** (the process called **glycogenesis**), and it inhibits the breakdown
of glycogen back to glucose. The net effect is to bring the blood sugar down.
Its absence or ineffectiveness is **diabetes mellitus**: glucose accumulates in the blood,
spills into the urine, and the tissues starve amid plenty.
The other options:
**(c) Adrenaline** ✗ does the **opposite** — it triggers **glycogenolysis**, breaking glycogen
down to glucose so that energy is available at once in an emergency. Insulin and adrenaline,
with glucagon, are the antagonistic pair that keep blood sugar steady.
**(a) Cortisone** ✗ is a steroid of the adrenal cortex; it raises blood glucose by promoting
gluconeogenesis, again the opposite direction.
**(b) Bile acids** ✗ are not hormones at all but emulsifying agents made in the liver, which
help digest **fats**.
Insulin is also the protein whose sequence Sanger first determined, and the first hormone
made by recombinant DNA technology.
∴ insulin.

India and in much of the world: a few parts per million of potassium iodate in table salt is

Deficiency of **vitamin C** causes **scurvy** ✓.
Vitamin C is **ascorbic acid** — the name itself means 'anti-scurvy' — and it is needed for
the synthesis of **collagen**, the protein that holds connective tissue together. Without it
the enzyme that hydroxylates proline cannot work, the collagen formed is defective, and the
tissues that depend on it fail: the gums swell and bleed, teeth loosen, wounds will not heal,
old scars reopen, and blood vessels become fragile so that bruises appear at the slightest
knock.

historical association with long sea voyages, where fresh food ran out. James Lind's
controlled trial of 1747 showed citrus fruit cured it, and the issue of lime juice to the
Royal Navy is why British sailors were called 'limeys'.
Sources are citrus fruits, amla, guava, tomatoes and green vegetables; the vitamin is easily
destroyed by heat, so overcooking removes it.
The other deficiencies named belong to other vitamins:
**(b) rickets** — vitamin **D**
**(c) pyorrhoea** — associated with vitamin C too, but scurvy is the defining disease
**(d) pernicious anaemia** — vitamin **B₁₂**

DNA contains **four** bases:
**purines** — adenine and guanine
**pyrimidines** — cytosine and **thymine**
RNA contains the same first three but replaces thymine with **uracil**.

Thymine and uracil differ by a single **methyl group**: thymine is **5-methyluracil**. That
one small difference is not accidental. **Cytosine deaminates spontaneously to uracil** at a
slow but constant rate, and if uracil were a legitimate DNA base the repair enzymes would
have no way of telling such damage from genuine sequence. Because DNA uses thymine instead,
any uracil found in DNA is recognised immediately as damage and cut out by the enzyme uracil
DNA glycosylase.
RNA, which is transcribed afresh as needed and then degraded, has no such requirement for
fidelity over time, and uses the simpler and cheaper uracil.
The mirror-image question — which base is in RNA but not DNA — has the answer **thymine**,
and the two are easily confused, so it is worth reading the question carefully.
∴ uracil.

A molecule is chiral if it contains a chiral centre, so the question is which part of a
nucleic acid provides one.
Take the three components of a nucleotide:
**The phosphate group** — tetrahedral, but with two of its oxygens equivalent in the
phosphodiester backbone. **Not chiral** ✗, which rules out (d).
**The bases** — adenine, guanine, cytosine, thymine and uracil are all **flat, planar**
heterocyclic rings. A planar molecule has a plane of symmetry and cannot be chiral ✗, which
rules out (c).
**The sugar** ✓ — **ribose** in RNA and **2′-deoxyribose** in DNA. Each is a pentose with
several **asymmetric carbon atoms**, and in nature both occur exclusively in the **D** form.
That is the source of the chirality ✓ — option (a).
Option (b) is wrong only in the letter: the sugar is **D**, not L. Nature's nucleic acids are
built from D-sugars just as its proteins are built from L-amino acids — a consistency whose
origin is still debated but whose consequence is clear: every nucleic acid on Earth twists
the same way.
That uniform handedness is precisely why the DNA double helix is **right-handed**. A
hypothetical L-sugar backbone would give a left-handed helix, and the two could not pair
with each other.
∴ D-sugar component.

The sugars are the defining chemical difference between the two nucleic acids, and the names
record it:
**RNA** = **ribo**nucleic acid, containing **ribose**
**DNA** = **deoxyribo**nucleic acid, containing **2′-deoxyribose**

The prefix **deoxy-** means 'lacking an oxygen', and the **2′** says where: the hydroxyl at
carbon 2′ of the ribose ring is replaced by a plain **hydrogen**. That is the only structural
difference between the two sugars.
Its consequence is large. The 2′-hydroxyl of RNA can attack the neighbouring phosphodiester
bond, so **RNA is readily hydrolysed**, especially in alkali. DNA, lacking that hydroxyl,
is far more **stable** — which is exactly what is wanted of a molecule that must preserve
genetic information for the lifetime of an organism and pass it on unchanged. RNA, by
contrast, is made and destroyed continually, and its instability is an advantage.
The distractors all introduce **arabinose**, which is a C-2 epimer of ribose and occurs in
neither nucleic acid. (It appears in the antiviral drug cytarabine, precisely because the
wrong sugar jams the machinery.)

**C-1′** — the base
**C-3′** — the link to the next nucleotide
**C-5′** — the phosphate

**Chargaff's rule**, established by Erwin Chargaff in the late 1940s from careful analysis of
DNA from many organisms, states that in any DNA sample:
**amount of adenine = amount of thymine** (A = T)
**amount of guanine = amount of cytosine** (G = C)
which is option **(a)** ✓
Equivalently, the total **purines equal the total pyrimidines**: A + G = T + C.
The rule looked like a curious numerical coincidence at the time, and its explanation came
only with the **double helix** in 1953. The two strands are **complementary**: adenine pairs
with thymine through **two** hydrogen bonds, and guanine with cytosine through **three**. Every
A on one strand faces a T on the other, so their totals must be equal — and likewise for G
and C.
Chargaff's figures were in fact one of the crucial pieces of evidence Watson and Crick used,
because any proposed structure had to explain them.
Note what the rule does **not** say: A need not equal G. The A+T to G+C ratio varies widely
between organisms — human DNA is about 60 % A+T, while some bacteria are 70 % G+C — which is
why option (d), 'all bases equal', is wrong.
Options (b) and (c) pair the bases wrongly: a purine must pair with a pyrimidine, since two
purines would be too wide for the helix and two pyrimidines too narrow.
∴ option (a).

In the DNA double helix the two strands are held together by hydrogen bonds between
**complementary** bases, and the pairing is fixed:
**adenine with thymine** (A–T), joined by **two** hydrogen bonds
**guanine with cytosine** (G–C), joined by **three** hydrogen bonds
which is option **(c)** ✓
Two constraints force this pattern.
**Size.** A purine (adenine, guanine) is a double ring and a pyrimidine (thymine, cytosine) a
single ring. Pairing purine with pyrimidine keeps the width of the helix **constant** at
about 20 Å along its whole length. Two purines would bulge and two pyrimidines would pinch.
That rules out (a), which pairs the two purines together and the two pyrimidines together.
**Hydrogen bonding.** The donor and acceptor groups must line up. Adenine's arrangement fits
thymine exactly and guanine's fits cytosine; the other combinations do not match.
Options (b) and (d) both bring in **uracil**, which occurs in **RNA**, not DNA — a different
error, and the one the question is chiefly testing.
The pairing is also what makes **replication** possible: separate the strands and each
specifies its partner uniquely, so one molecule becomes two identical ones. It is the
structural fact from which the whole of molecular genetics follows.
∴ adenine and thymine; guanine and cytosine.

The **central dogma** of molecular biology, as stated by Francis Crick in 1958, is that
genetic information flows
**DNA ⟶ RNA ⟶ Proteins** ✓ — option (c)
The two steps have names:
**Transcription** — DNA ⟶ RNA. One strand of the DNA is copied into a complementary strand
of messenger RNA by RNA polymerase, in the nucleus.
**Translation** — RNA ⟶ Protein. The mRNA is read at the ribosome in **triplets (codons)**,
each specifying one amino acid, and the polypeptide chain is assembled in that order.
So the information held in the base sequence of DNA ends up as the amino acid sequence of a
protein, and it is that sequence which determines the protein's shape and therefore
everything it does.
The word 'dogma' records Crick's claim about what **cannot** happen: information does not
flow back from protein to nucleic acid. That part has held. What has been added since is
**reverse transcription**, DNA made from RNA by retroviruses such as HIV — a flow backwards
along the first arrow, but not from protein.
The distractors each break the chain in a different place: (a) runs it backwards, and (b) and
(d) insert **carbohydrates**, which carry no sequence information and play no part in the
flow.
∴ DNA ⟶ RNA ⟶ Proteins.
